title: Lazy Reset Simulation with Version Tracking
approach_explanation: The problem requires us to simulate array updates where a value exceeding $h$ resets the entire array to its initial state. A naive simulation of resetting all $n$ elements upon every crash would lead to an $O(n 	imes m)$ time complexity, which is too slow and results in Time Limit Exceeded (TLE). Instead, we use a lazy reset approach with version tracking. We maintain a global `current_reset` counter that increments every time a crash happens. Each element keeps track of the last reset version it was synchronized with (`last_reset`). When an operation updates an element, we first check if its value is outdated (i.e., its last synchronized version is older than `current_reset`). If so, we lazily restore it to its initial value from the original array `arr` and update its version. Then, we perform the addition. If the new value exceeds $h$, we simply increment `current_reset` instead of resetting the whole array. After processing all operations, any element with a version older than `current_reset` defaults to its original value.

code_breakdown.explanation: Read test cases, array size $n$, number of operations $m$, and limit $h$. Read the initial array elements into `arr`, copy them into `temp`, and initialize the `last_reset` version tracking array to all zeros along with `current_reset = 0`.

Iterate through each of the $m$ operations. For an operation on index $b-1$, check if the element has been reset since its last update. If `last_reset[b-1] < current_reset`, restore `temp[b-1]` to `arr[b-1]` and update `last_reset[b-1]` to `current_reset`.
Check if adding $c$ to `temp[b-1]` exceeds $h$. If it does not, safely add $c$. If it does, trigger a global crash by incrementing `current_reset` without explicitly modifying the entire array.

Iterate through each element of the array. If an element's version `last_reset[i]` is less than `current_reset`, it means it was never updated after the latest global reset, so we output its original value `arr[i]`. Otherwise, we output its accumulated value `temp[i]`.

complexity_analysis.time_justification: Reading the input array takes $O(n)$ time. Processing $m$ operations takes $O(m)$ time because each operation involves constant-time checks and updates thanks to lazy version tracking. Final output takes $O(n)$ time. Summing over all test cases, the total time complexity is $O(\sum n + \sum m)$, comfortably fitting within the 2.0-second time limit for $2 \cdot 10^5$ elements.
complexity_analysis.space_justification: We allocate auxiliary vectors `arr`, `temp`, and `last_reset`, each of size $n$, per test case. Thus, the auxiliary space complexity is linear with respect to the array size $n$, taking $O(n)$ space which uses well within the 256 MB limit.

strengths: Clever lazy evaluation strategy avoiding $O(n \times m)$ overhead.
Clean separation of original array and working array.
edge_cases_handled: Operations where the values instantly exceed $h$ on the first addition.
Elements that are never touched by any operation.
Multiple consecutive crashes affecting elements selectively.
best_practices_feedback: Use `std::ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(NULL);` for faster I/O in competitive programming.
Prefer `\n` over `endl` to avoid unnecessary buffer flushes.

Use `long long` for array elements or increments if $a_i + c_i$ can overflow standard 32-bit signed integers (though given $h, c_i \le 10^9$, standard 32-bit signed integers fit values up to $2 \cdot 10^9$, which fits inside standard `int`, but `long long` is safer).

optimization_and_alternatives.tradeoffs: A segment tree could handle range updates if the problem statement were generalized, but for point updates, it is unnecessarily complex and slower than the $O(n + m)$ version tracking approach.
